title: Christianity: the Lord's Prayer
hookLine: the prayer Jesus taught his followers (Matthew 6:9–13)

lines: OUR FATHER, WHO ART IN HEAVEN.
cards: Our Father, who art in heaven. Those six words travel a long way from any church: into school halls, hospital rooms, gravesides and old films.
Catholics, Orthodox Christians and Protestants all pray what follows, each in their own language and their own version, with small differences in the wording. It all began with a simple request.
In Luke's Gospel, the disciples watch Jesus pray and ask him: teach us.

teach.b: Matthew chapter six, in the King James Version: "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread."

teach.h: GOD'S NAME FIRST, THEN OUR BREAD.
teach.b: Then forgiveness, as we forgive others; then protection from temptation and evil. It's short on purpose: just before it, Jesus warns against heaping up words, as if length impressed God. Look at the shape.
The first half faces God: the name, the kingdom, the will. The second half faces us: bread, forgiveness, protection. Big things, then small things, allowed in the same breath.
The Greek word translated daily, epiousios, appears almost nowhere else in all of Greek writing, and nobody is certain what it means. Daily? For tomorrow?
Needed for existence? Early Christian writers already argued about it, and some read it as the bread of the Eucharist too.
However it's translated, the request is small: enough for today, not a year's supply.
It echoes the manna in the wilderness, from the story of the going out from Egypt: bread that came each morning, enough for that day, and spoiled if hoarded. The endings differ.
Many Protestants close with for thine is the kingdom, the power and the glory. Luke's version doesn't have that line, and at Catholic Mass it comes a little later, after another short prayer.

how: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians all pray the Lord's Prayer, many daily, and congregations often say it together; Catholics call it the Our Father and pray it in the rosary.

games.why: he gives a short prayer and warns against piling up words; the small needs come in the same breath as the great.

practice: Read it slowly once, pausing at each line; if you pray, you can pray it, and if not, simply listen to the old words: Our Father which art in heaven, hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come, give us this day our daily bread.
Then sit with that one line: what is enough, just for today?

wordCard.voice: Christianity, through the Lord's Prayer: the prayer Jesus taught, God's name first, then bread for today. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek of Matthew 6:11: daily, or for tomorrow; the meaning is debated.

carryVoice: Your line: daily bread. Enough for today; tomorrow's worries can wait. That's two hundred fifty-five.
